title: Stories from living off the grid: Staying connected in the Alaskan wilderness
summary: See how Starlink and Ooma StarDial could help a former Forest Service ranger stay connected off the grid in the Alaskan wilderness.
body_markdown:
Disconnecting from technology is one of the best benefits of going to a national forest, and there are few better places than Admiralty Island in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest.


With nearly a million acres and plenty of bears and bald eagles, Admiralty Island has much to offer. Its remoteness is the attraction, but it also makes connection incredibly difficult. Ooma spoke with a former U.S. Forest Service ranger about what the Alaskan island is like off the grid and how[StarDial](https://www.ooma.com/home-phone-service/starlink/stardial/) could keep you connected in case of an emergency.


## Truly remote


Admiralty Island is home to the native Tlingit people, who call the island Xootsnoowu, which means “Fortress of the Bears.” Most of the island is protected within the Admiralty Island National Monument and Kootznoowoo Wilderness, which means there are nearly a million acres of uncut forest.


The island is the seventh largest in the U.S., according to the[Forest Service](https://www.fs.usda.gov/r10/tongass/recreation/admiralty-island-national-monument-0) , with a community home to the local Tlingit called Angoon on the west side of the island. There are around 600 people on the island, most in the city of Angoon. The 2000 Census claims 650 live in Angoon while more recent estimates say 572.


There are around 1,600 brown bears, according to[Travel Alaska](https://www.travelalaska.com/destinations/parks-public-lands/admiralty-island-national-monument) , making it the highest concentration of brown bears anywhere in the world. And, as you can tell, there are more bears than people on the island.


It also has the world’s greatest concentration of nesting bald eagles, with roughly 5,000 living on Admiralty with a nest nearly every mile along the coastline of Seymour Canal. This makes Admiralty a popular destination for birding and bear watching, with the latter happening at the Pack Creek Bear Viewing Area.


There are only 13 Forest Service cabins scattered across Admiralty, with some overnight accommodations available in Angoon.


This is a truly remote island, with not much room to host large groups of visitors. This is great if you want to hunt, fish, view wildlife or just relax in a cabin with no one around, but it also brings an issue: staying connected.


## Connection issues


The former forest ranger told Ooma that the Forest Service would send a crew of four to six people to maintain roughly 26 miles of trails, fix cabins, cut firewood, dig outhouse holes and more. They would stay around 10 days.


The rangers would communicate with radios that used repeaters stationed at the top of mountains. If the repeaters went down they’d be out of contact. One time, the ranger had to communicate with someone and borrowed a cellphone. They climbed to the top of the mountain, up above the trees, and tried to connect to a tower on another island, Kake, to connect.


With the amount of untouched nature on the island, getting any kind of connection is difficult. If you run into danger you’re on your own. Even worse, you’re not likely to see another person while you’re on the island.


“You’re not going to see people,” the former ranger said. “There’s nobody out there. You won’t see anyone. If you hike these trails, you won’t come across anyone else, there’s just no one there.”


You won’t be able to get into contact with a park ranger. Most people who visit the islands are locals from nearby Juneau, Alaska and know what to expect. There are some tourists who are anxious about being remote and overprepare. Without reliable communication, visitors need to plan more carefully before heading into the wilderness.


But what do you do if you run into an emergency? All the preparedness in the world can’t save you if you, or your family back home, run into an emergency that requires outside communication.


## Staying connected with StarDial


Using radios or smartphones on Admiralty Island is difficult due to the lack of infrastructure. As a national monument, Admiralty Island is protected from development. The repeaters on neighboring islands are likely the closest it’ll get to real communication infrastructure.


One way around that is with StarDial, which uses Starlink to connect your phone to the internet, allowing you to make calls and stay connected in an emergency.


“If I still had my cabin, I’d bring Starlink,” the former ranger told us. Because Starlink is easy to set up, taking just minutes, it’s a breeze to take with you on that floatplane and set up in.


The former ranger, however, pointed out to us that Admiralty is heavily forested, which makes placing the Starlink a little difficult. You’d have to set it up on the flat coastline near the cabins and use it — if you need to — when you’re at your cabin. Either way, having that peace of mind can be essential.


As Kevin Gomez, the[Starlink-equipped overlanding YouTuber behind Amp’d Adventures](https://www.ooma.com/blog/home-phone/overlanding-with-starlink/) , told us, you never know when you could eat a berry you’re not supposed to.
